pieces.question: Which level does your state fall into?

pieces.caption: states ask for a portfolio or formal assessment

alt: A choice card asking which of four levels a state falls into, None, Low, Moderate or High, beside a card showing nine states in the high group.
caption: The four levels the table sorts every state into. Confirm yours at the source, since laws change.

pieces.eyebrow: Four columns that earn their place

pieces.text: Hours, color coding, and a paragraph per child per day.

alt: A table of the four record keeping columns, Date, Subject, What part and How it went, with example entries, next to a note on what to leave off.
caption: An example entry for each of the four columns. Copy it into whatever you already open every day.

pieces.text: Include ordinary work, not only your best. Two points in the year beat one good week.

alt: A checklist of the five things a homeschool portfolio typically holds, beside a note about including ordinary work from more than one point in the year.
caption: The five things a homeschool portfolio usually holds, from the guide's own checklist.

steps.what: One line per week you can place
Before rebuilding any more than that

alt: A table showing what workbook pages, photos, library history and receipts can rebuild, beside a four-step evening plan for catching up on homeschool records.
caption: An example of what four kinds of evidence can rebuild, and the evening plan for using them.

alt: A four-row table pairing each check result, solid, mixed, worth another look, not enough to say, with what to do next.
caption: The four results of a short check, and what each one means for what happens next.

steps.what: Meeting time, place, what they want to see
One early, one recent, same subject
One folder, in the order they'll open it

alt: A checklist of what to bring to a homeschool evaluation, log, samples, materials list, attendance, and a note per subject, beside a four-step evening prep plan.
caption: What to bring, and the evening plan for pulling it together, from the guide.

pieces.title: Log it, don't rebuild it
items: A line on what you covered
Hours, only if yours counts them

pieces.text: Reconstructing a year of days from memory in June rarely works. Log it live.

alt: A checklist card listing a date, what was covered, and hours only if the state counts them, beside a note about logging live rather than rebuilding a year later.
caption: The three-part record that holds up whether your state counts days, hours, or nothing at all.

pieces.text: Record right after the lesson. An hour later, it's memory, not a record.

alt: A checklist card listing the date, subject and position, and one word on how it went, beside a note to record right after the lesson rather than from memory.
caption: The three things a homeschool record needs every time, nothing more.

pieces.text: Rules change. Check your own state's page before you toss anything.

alt: A small table showing what to keep and for how long: worksheets a handful, test results and the parent's own log kept permanently, and Florida's two-year portfolio law, next to a note to check your...
caption: Retention windows from HSLDA's general guidance and Florida's own statute.

pieces.eyebrow: How a subject lands on the week
Decide it before you need it
items: On a short day: two things
On a very short day: one thing
What we drop first: decided now

alt: A table showing which weekdays a subject lands on by days per week, one to five, beside a checklist for what a short day and a very short day include.
caption: Homeschooling Companion's own weekday pattern, and the short-day list worth deciding in advance.

pieces.text: Set to 4 and it runs Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday.

alt: A table splitting subject days across a four-day week, Math at four days down to Geography at one, beside a note on how a four-day subject runs in the app.
caption: Example: one way to split subject days across a four-day week.

alt: A card comparing Florida's one-time district filing with New Mexico's annual state filing, beside a checklist of what a notice of intent usually asks for.
caption: Two real states, shown as examples of how a notice of intent can differ.

pieces.text: Mark a day as you go. A box ticked on the day beats a June reconstruction.

alt: A card comparing Pennsylvania's 180-day or 900-hour rule with Texas's no-count rule, beside a note to mark each day as you go if yours counts.
caption: Two real states, shown as examples of the two patterns: a set count, and no count at all.

steps.what: Date, subject, one word on how it went

pieces.text: A withdrawal letter and a records request are different documents.

alt: A timeline of the first-month order: find your state's rules, withdraw and request records, file what's due, then start a plain record on day one.
caption: Example: one order to move through in the first month of homeschooling.

pieces.text: 400 lessons and 400 notes shared by the whole household, not per child.

alt: Two homeschool record cards side by side, one per child, each logging the same shared history lesson separately with its own note and a different math entry.
caption: A shared morning logged once per child, example.

pieces.text: Abandoned books belong on the list. It says what did not work, not just what did.

alt: A three-column homeschool reading log card showing a book title, the date it was started, and the date it was finished or marked stopped, for three example books.
caption: Book, started, finished or stopped: the three columns, example rows.

steps.what: Teach it first, not last in the day
Fewer problems or pages, same subject
Check the skill right before this one
Only after the first three come back clean

alt: A four-step timeline: change the time of day, then the amount, then go back one step, then look at new material last.
caption: The order to try when a subject stalls. Example: long division, in the guide.
